title: The replication crisis, ten years on

turns.speaker: Gareth
turns.text: Another textbook effect failed to replicate this month. That's three this year from the same chapter.

turns.speaker: Gareth
turns.text: Social priming. Most of it has quietly evaporated.

turns.speaker: Hana
turns.text: The large replication project got something like thirty-nine per cent of psychology findings to hold up. That number is a decade old and people still find it shocking.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Is thirty-nine actually bad, though? A field where everything replicates is a field taking no risks.

turns.speaker: Hana
turns.text: That's a fair point and it gets made too rarely. The problem isn't the failure rate, it's that the failures were invisible.

turns.speaker: Gareth
turns.text: Because nobody could publish them. A null result was a wasted three years.

turns.speaker: Gareth
turns.text: So the literature was a record of what worked once, not of what was tried.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Pre-registration seems to have helped, at least. You say what you'll test before you look.

turns.speaker: Hana
turns.text: It has. Registered reports show far lower rates of positive findings, which is exactly what you'd expect if the old rate was inflated.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: The incentive underneath it hasn't moved though. Careers still run on novel and surprising.

turns.speaker: Gareth
turns.text: And a replication, however careful, counts for almost nothing at a hiring committee.

turns.speaker: Hana
turns.text: Which is the actual fix and it's the one nobody controls.

points: Several textbook psychology effects, particularly in social priming, have failed to replicate.
A major replication project found about thirty-nine per cent of findings held up.
Theo argues a low failure rate would indicate a field taking no risks, so the rate itself is not the problem.
Hana and Gareth identify the real problem as invisibility, since null results were unpublishable and the literature recorded only what worked once.
Pre-registration and registered reports have reduced positive findings, consistent with the old rate being inflated.
The underlying incentive remains, as careers reward novelty and replication counts for little in hiring.
